description: Redaction configuration via obs.redaction.regex_patterns and obs.redaction.sensitive_keys. Replaces the legacy hardcoded _secret_ key prefix. PROTOCOL_SPEC 10.6.1 governs the matching: `sensitive_keys` is a per-entry hybrid — an entry containing `*` or `?` is a glob-dialect pattern matched with algorithm A25 (anchored to the whole field name), an entry containing neither is a case-insensitive substring match against the normalized name; `regex_patterns` is an UNANCHORED, case-insensitive SEARCH over the string form of the value. The 'full regex match' this description claimed until v1.37.0 described no implementation — all three search — and every regex case here was anchored with ^...$, so the corpus could not tell. trace_id, caller_id, target_id, module_id and span_id MUST NEVER be redacted. See docs/features/redaction.md#configured-rules-obsredaction.

expected._note: Even when patterns/keys would match, correlation fields MUST appear unmodified.

test_cases.scenario: The canonical `obs.redaction.sensitive_keys` MUST be the key an implementation reads. Nothing else in this fixture pins WHICH key path is consulted, which is how apcore-rust read only the legacy `observability.redaction.*` path undetected: an operator following the documentation had their redaction config silently discarded, with no warning and no error (apcore-rust#32).

Each SDK MUST still honour the pre-canonical spelling IT SHIPPED, with a ONE-SHOT deprecation warning naming the legacy key and its canonical replacement. The legacy spelling is per-SDK history, NOT a cross-language contract: apcore-rust shipped `observability.redaction.sensitive_keys`, apcore-typescript shipped `observability.redaction.field_patterns`, and apcore-python never had an `observability.*` namespace at all. An earlier revision of this case hard-coded Rust's spelling, so it was satisfiable by apcore-rust alone — the same defect this fixture exists to catch, committed inside the fixture itself.
test_cases.skip_when_legacy_key_is_null: apcore-python MUST NOT gain the fallback. No Python deployment ever had that spelling honoured, so adding it creates a deprecated surface for zero users — and it is a security-relevant regression: a stale `observability.redaction.sensitive_keys: []` would flip from 'ignored, defaults apply' to 'key-based redaction disabled'. A driver whose `legacy_key_by_sdk` entry is null MUST skip with that reason, not xfail as though the SDK were deficient.

test_cases.scenario: When both spellings are present the canonical one MUST win. Drivers whose SDK has no legacy spelling skip this case — see `legacy_config_key_is_honoured_with_a_deprecation_warning`.

test_cases._why: DISCRIMINATING — apcore-rust lowercases the KEY (`p.matches(name) || p.matches(&name.to_lowercase())`) but never the PATTERN, so an operator who writes any capitalised spelling gets redaction in Python and TypeScript and PLAINTEXT in Rust, with no warning: the pattern is valid and simply matches nothing. PROTOCOL_SPEC 10.6.1 requires the fold on BOTH sides. Note the shape of the bug — `*key*` matches `API_KEY` in all three today, so a case spelled in lower case cannot see it; only an UPPERCASE PATTERN discriminates.

DISCRIMINATING against all three, in two opposite directions. `[!p]assword` contains no `*` and no `?`, so under 10.6.1 it is a SUBSTRING entry and matches only a field whose name contains it literally. Today: apcore-python (fnmatch) and apcore-rust (glob::Pattern) read `[!p]` as 'any character except p' and redact `bassword`; apcore-typescript passes `[!p]` verbatim into a RegExp, where it means '! or p', and redacts `password` — the exact field the other two deliberately exclude. The meaning is inverted, not merely weakened (#117 section 1).

Separates the two branches of the hybrid. `key` (no metacharacter) is a SUBSTRING entry and matches `api_key`; `key*` is a PATTERN entry, anchored, and matches neither `api_key` nor `my_keyring`. An implementation that treats every entry as a substring, or every entry as a pattern, fails one half of this case.

Pins the correction to this fixture's own description. Every pre-v1.37.0 regex case here was spelled ^...$, which is satisfied by a full match and by a search alike, so the corpus could not distinguish them — while all three SDKs have always searched (re.search / RegExp.test / Regex::is_match). An implementation that switched to a full match to satisfy the old description would pass every previous case and fail this one.

DISCRIMINATING — apcore-python's log-emission path (`_apply_redaction_config`) passed the value through `str(value)` before searching, while its OWN executor-capture path (`redact_sensitive`), apcore-typescript (`typeof value === 'string'`) and apcore-rust (`Value::String(s)`) all test strings only. Measured: with these patterns `amount: 42` came back `***REDACTED***` from one Python surface and `42` from the other — one SDK, two answers, on a rule 10.6 requires to hold on both. PROTOCOL_SPEC 10.6.1 requirement 2 now forbids the conversion outright, because it cannot be specified: `True`/`true`/`true` and `{'a': 1}`/`[object Object]`/`{"a":1}` are three renderings of one value. This fixture's pre-existing `regex_pattern_value_match` case already carried `amount: 42`, but next to patterns anchored on `Bearer` and `sk-` that cannot match "42" under any reading — a case that cannot fail against any implementation pins nothing.

The negative above must not be over-read into 'containers are exempt'. 10.6.1 requirement 2 says containers are DESCENDED INTO, so a string at its own position inside an object or an array is still tested — an implementation that satisfied the previous case by skipping any non-string field wholesale, rather than by declining to stringify it, fails here.
D-152, the shape an optional field takes (`Secret | None` puts the marker in anyOf[0]). `note` is the control on the same object.

D-152: a value described by several branches is redacted when ANY of them marks it; the walk does not decide which branch matched. The value is an integer, matching the UNMARKED branch — an implementation that redacts only when the marked branch validates leaks it.
D-152: a property declared inside a combinator branch is a field of the object like one declared directly. `code` sits in the sibling branch, unmarked, and stays visible.
The over-correction guard: a field whose branches carry no marker is not sensitive because it is a union. A marked field whose value is null stays null.

driver_contract.discriminating_payload: `username` matches NO entry of the canonical default list; `password` and `_secret_token` both do. That is what makes these cases able to tell 'the override was read and replaced the defaults' from 'the defaults are in force'. A payload whose keys all match a default anyway — such as this fixture's existing `auth_header`, which contains `auth` — stays green under both, and is why the config-key defect went unnoticed in every SDK.
driver_contract.which_key_is_read_is_part_of_the_contrac: Behaviour-given-a-config is not enough. Drivers MUST build the config from the exact dot-path the case names and assert the resulting redaction, so that reading the wrong key path fails here rather than in an operator's production logs.
driver_contract.legacy_spelling_is_per_sdk_history: The CANONICAL key `obs.redaction.*` is the cross-language contract and every SDK MUST read it — that is `canonical_config_key_is_read`, and it applies to all three. The LEGACY spelling is not: each SDK carries whatever it shipped before D-53, and apcore-python carries nothing. Drivers read `legacy_key_by_sdk` for their own language; a `null` entry means the case does not apply and MUST be skipped with that reason stated, not xfailed as though the SDK were deficient.
driver_contract.a_case_must_carry_its_own_inputs: Every config-key case names BOTH the key to write (`legacy_key_by_sdk` / `config_canonical`) and the value to write (`legacy_value` / the value inside `config_canonical`). An earlier revision named the key and dropped the value, which forces each driver to invent one — and a driver-invented input is not a cross-language contract, it is three private guesses that happen to agree today.
driver_contract.non_string_values_are_not_stringified: A driver MUST feed the `input` object through its SDK's redaction with the value TYPES intact — a driver that JSON-serialises the case and reloads it as text, or that coerces every leaf to a string before calling, makes `regex_patterns_do_not_test_non_string_values` unable to fail and re-creates the blind spot that hid the defect. The distinction under test is exactly whether the implementation converts, so the conversion must not happen in the harness (PROTOCOL_SPEC 10.6.1 requirement 2).
driver_contract.schema_marked_fields: Cases carrying `schema` exercise the `x-sensitive` rule (PROTOCOL_SPEC 10.6, A13) alongside the configured rules: pass `schema` as the schema the redaction walks — the same entry point the executor's input capture uses (apcore-python `redact_sensitive(data, schema, ...)`, and its equivalents). Their `redaction_config` disables every configured rule, and no field name in them matches a default sensitive key, so each redaction in `expected` can only come from an `x-sensitive` marker. D-152: the walk descends into `anyOf` / `oneOf` / `allOf` branches; before it, no SDK did, so an optional field (`Secret | None`) was captured and logged in plain text.
